subject: chemistry
title: Life cycle assessment
key_idea: A life cycle assessment (LCA) compares the environmental impact of a product at each stage of its life: raw materials, manufacture, use and disposal. Energy, water and resources can be measured. The effect of pollutants needs value judgements, so an LCA is not purely objective.

sections.heading: What a life cycle assessment is

blocks.text: A life cycle assessment (LCA) judges the effect a product has on the environment during its whole life. This section covers the stages and what is measured.

items.meaning: A comparison of the environmental impact of a product at each stage of its life.
The total carbon dioxide released over the whole life of a product, not just when it is used.

diagram.alt: The stages of a life cycle assessment in order: raw materials, manufacture and packaging, use and operation, disposal.
steps: Disposal at end of useful life

blocks.text: Transport and distribution are considered at every stage.
What is measured at each stage

items: Raw materials: the resources used and the energy needed to extract and process them.
Manufacture: the energy and water used to make and package the product.
Use: the energy needed to operate it, and to clean or repair it. A reusable product may be used many times.
Disposal: whether it can be recycled or reused, whether it is biodegradable, and the landfill space it takes up.
An LCA covers four stages: raw materials, manufacture, use and disposal.
The carbon footprint of a product is more than the emissions when it is used.

blocks.text: LCAs are used to compare products, for example a glass bottle and a polymer bottle. This section covers what can be measured and what cannot.
Easy to measure and harder to measure

items: Use of water, resources, energy and some wastes can be fairly easily quantified.
Giving a number to the effect of a pollutant is less straightforward. It needs value judgements.
So an LCA is not a purely objective process.

diagram.alt: Sort each item into easily quantified or needs a value judgement.
diagram.prompt: Which items in an LCA can be fairly easily quantified?

items.text: Energy used to make a bottle
Water used to wash a reusable bottle
Deciding how harmful one pollutant is compared with another
Giving a number to the effect of a pollutant

items: Compare the products stage by stage using the data given, for example total energy to process and manufacture.
Use ratios or percentages where the data allows, such as the percentage recycled.
A reusable product spreads its impact over every use.
Finish with a judgement that is supported by the reasons you have given.
A selective or abbreviated LCA looks at only some stages or some data.
It can be misused to reach a conclusion decided in advance, for example in advertising.
Energy, water, resources and some wastes can be quantified.
Pollutant effects need value judgements, so an LCA is not purely objective.
Abbreviated LCAs can be misused to support advertising claims.

checks.q: Name the four stages of a life cycle assessment of a product.
checks.a: Extracting and processing raw materials; manufacturing and packaging; use and operation; disposal at the end of its useful life.

checks.q: Explain why carbon dioxide emitted when a car is used is not its total carbon footprint.
checks.a: Carbon dioxide is also released when raw materials are extracted and processed, when the car is manufactured and when it is disposed of.

checks.q: Explain why an LCA is not a purely objective process.
checks.a: Water, energy, resources and some wastes can be measured, but giving a number to the effect of a pollutant needs value judgements.

worked_example.question:
Emissions from cars contain carbon dioxide.

Explain why carbon dioxide emissions during use and operation are not the total carbon footprint for a car.

Refer to the stages of the life cycle assessment of a car in your answer.
answer_points: Carbon dioxide is emitted when raw materials are extracted or processed.
Carbon dioxide is emitted during manufacturing.
Carbon dioxide is emitted during disposal at the end of the car's useful life.
worked_example.tip: One mark for each stage other than use and operation.

worked_example.question:
A life-cycle assessment is an analysis of the overall environmental impact that a product may have throughout its lifetime.

A company does a life-cycle assessment to investigate two possible materials for making a single-use takeaway food container.

Table 18.1 gives some of the information the company uses.

| | Aluminium | Poly(propene) |
| Mass of raw materials (g) | 8 | 31.5 |
| Energy used (MJ / kg) | 61 | 73 |
| Percentage recycled (%) | 54 | 11 |
| Cost per kg (£) | 1.40 | 0.98 |

The company decides to use aluminium to make the food container.

Explain why using aluminium is better than using poly(propene).

Use information from Table 18.1.
answer_points: Aluminium uses a smaller mass of raw materials (8 g compared with 31.5 g).
A higher percentage of aluminium is recycled (54% compared with 11%).
Aluminium uses less energy (61 MJ/kg compared with 73 MJ/kg).
Overall cost per container is less for aluminium, because the mass is so much smaller.
worked_example.tip: Any three. The comparison must be stated, not just the figures.
